source.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
source.authors: Javier Ferrando; O. Obeso; Senthooran Rajamanoharan; Neel Nanda

record.file_problem: Minor PDF-text extraction artifacts appear, but the paper and appendices are present and usable.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies SAE-based feature analysis to Gemma and Llama language models and reports results bearing on the LLM-specific indirect-evidence version; it does not reproduce the toy-model superposition experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper measures entity-recognition SAE activations and reports their separation across entity types and layers, along with activation frequencies. These bear on V4's claim that SAEs can recover sparse features in LLMs. Refusal steering, weight orthogonalization, attention effects, and explicit uncertainty steering are not recorded as rows because their outcome measures concern behavior or attention rather than SAE feature recovery or superposition geometry.
record.test_reason: The paper uses pretrained Gemma Scope and LlamaScope SAEs as an interpretability tool to find entity-recognition and uncertainty latents. Its results concern knowledge awareness: separation of known from unknown entities, steering of refusals, and attention effects. It does not test whether features in LLMs are in superposition or spread across neurons. It also does not test whether SAEs recover a model's features in general, or the toy-model and canonicity claims. Finding a few useful latents with an SAE presupposes V4 rather than testing it, so it is T4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also stress causal claims the paraphrase omits. Steering these base-model SAE directions controls knowledge refusal and hallucination in the chat model, suggesting fine-tuning repurposes an existing mechanism. Unknown-entity directions suppress the attention of attribute-extraction heads. Uncertainty latents discriminate correct from mistaken answers.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses pretrained SAEs to identify entity-recognition and uncertainty latents in LLMs, rather than training toy networks with controlled sparse features and measuring their superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The best entity-recognition separation is concentrated in intermediate layers; results are reported across model sizes and entity types. The paper notes less pronounced effects for some Llama and Gemma 2 9B analyses.

fits_no_version.finding: Single SAE latents, from SAEs trained on base models, fire almost only on known or on unknown entities across four entity types. Separation peaks in middle layers. Steering with these latents shifts refusal in chat models; weaker effects appear in Gemma 2 9B and Llama 3.1 8B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents in base LLMs encode entity knowledge-awareness directions that transfer causally to chat-model refusal behaviour.

fits_no_version.finding: An SAE latent at the end-of-instruction token separates correct from mistaken answers (73.2 AUROC, F1 72) in Gemma 2B IT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents can act as uncertainty signals that predict factual errors.

record.problems: The authors acknowledge possible inaccuracies in known/unknown labels: models may guess attributes without knowing an entity or fail to recall selected attributes despite knowing it. Intermediate cases are discarded. Several separation results are figure-only, and the authors note possible overlap between post-cutoff song titles and pretraining data.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant results were omitted under the 60-row limit. Refusal, attention, and steering outcomes were not extracted because their measures do not directly assess SAE feature recovery or superposition geometry.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity transitions or geometry.
No analysis of neuron polysemanticity or capacity allocation.
No measure of how features spread over neurons. No test of whether SAE recovery reflects superposition; SAEs are assumed as a tool.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE latents.

record.verdict_notes: The paper mentions superposition only in its background on SAEs. Its results presuppose that SAE dictionaries recover meaningful features. The Llama and Gemma 2 9B steering effects are weaker, per the authors. Table 9 and the Figure 28 legends disagree on Gemma 2 2B activation frequencies (0.006/0.005 vs 0.008/0.008).

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometric structure.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise from limited capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons can arise without capacity pressure, and whether they evidence superposition.

The paper examines SAE-recovered entity-recognition and uncertainty features, not whether features are spread across many neurons; it does not establish the general prevalence of such features in LLMs.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model's representation.
Whether the underlying represented features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.operation_detail: Measured layerwise known-entity latent separation scores, including top latents and the cross-entity MaxMin score.
rows.measure: Known-entity latent separation score across layers
rows.value: figure only; the text says separation scores rise through the model, peak around layer 9, and then plateau; middle layers provide the best-performing latents.
rows.uncertainty: Error bars show maximum and minimum scores.
rows.note: Top-5 latents and a MaxMin score are shown; numerical values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Separation score of selected SAE latents for known vs unknown entities. This measures the study's own feature-search result, not superposition or SAE feature recovery as such.

rows.baseline: All-token probability distribution shown for comparison; numeric baseline not stated.

rows.check: Control against the token-likelihood confound for the study's own interpretation, not a V4 measure. Table 9 gives frequency 0.006, but the Figure 28 legend shows 0.008.

rows.subject: Gemma 2B IT
rows.operation_detail: Selected an SAE latent using training-set differences between correct and mistaken answers, then evaluated it on test data.
rows.measure: Test-set discrimination of correct versus mistaken answers using the selected latent
rows.note: This is an additional SAE-latent finding about answer uncertainty, not the known/unknown entity-recognition feature.
rows.check: AUROC of an uncertainty latent used as an error classifier. This is the study's own method performance; the subject is Gemma 2B IT (Gemma 1) with a community SAE.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma 2 2B and 9B, and Llama 3.1 8B; tested entity-recognition features and datasets
reader_labels.reason: SAE latents show entity-type separation, layerwise concentration in intermediate layers, and differing known/unknown activation rates on post-cutoff songs; token-probability correlations are described as negligible overall (F1–F6, P1–P6, L1–L6).
